# Study specification and scientific boundaries

**Aim:** demonstrate defensible R workflows on **invented breast cancer data**, not estimate any genuine cancer effect. Every row and value is generated in this document. Subtype, tumor size, ERBB2 score, toxicity, response, survival, person-time, and longitudinal measures are fictional. The quantities, effects and directions are **not validated clinical patterns**. Continuous ERBB2 values are arbitrary teaching scores, not raw gene counts, normalized RNA-seq data or a clinical HER2 assay. The synthetic study uses one baseline row per invented patient; the longitudinal dataset has multiple records per patient and is modeled separately.

**Study estimands:** mean ERBB2 difference by subtype; grade-specific ERBB2 score comparisons; response odds ratio; toxicity event rate ratio; within-patient outcome change; hazard ratio for an illustrative time-to-event endpoint; held-out prediction discrimination; and exploratory multi-feature associations. None of these are causal effects. No experiment or randomized treatment allocation is represented.

**Before applying to actual research:** replace synthetic generation with approved inputs and a validated dictionary; establish design, eligibility, patient-specimen cardinality, assay, provenance, transformations, missing-data mechanism, sampling and endpoints. In particular, a subtype classification based on the same gene cannot be used to claim independent confirmation of that gene association.

# 01 Environment and fixed seed

```{r setup, include=TRUE}
## 01.01 Explicit, minimal dependencies; never install mid-knit
required <- c("knitr", "ggplot2")
missing_packages <- required[!vapply(required, requireNamespace, logical(1), quietly=TRUE)]
if (length(missing_packages)) stop("Missing packages: ", paste(missing_packages, collapse=", "))
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo=TRUE, message=FALSE, warning=TRUE)
set.seed(params$seed)

## 01.02 Standard Paul’s Notes / Okabe-Ito palette
pal <- c("Luminal-like"="#0072B2", "Basal-like"="#D55E00")
fmt <- function(x, digits=3) format(round(x, digits), nsmall=digits, trim=TRUE)
present <- function(x, title, digits=3) {
  knitr::kable(x, digits=digits, caption=title, row.names=FALSE)
}
```

# 02 Synthetic data and machine-checkable dictionary

```{r synthetic-cohort}
## 02.01 One synthetic subject and one synthetic baseline specimen per row
n <- 240L
patient_id <- sprintf("S%04d", seq_len(n))
subtype <- factor(rep(c("Luminal-like", "Basal-like"), each=n/2L),
                  levels=names(pal))
age_years <- pmin(89, pmax(25, round(stats::rnorm(n, 59, 12))))
tumor_cm <- pmax(0.2, stats::rlnorm(n, log(2.5), 0.38))
erbb2_score <- stats::rnorm(n, mean=ifelse(subtype=="Basal-like", 11, 14),
                           sd=ifelse(subtype=="Basal-like", 3.8, 3.0))
grade <- factor(sample(c("I", "II", "III"), n, replace=TRUE,
                       prob=c(0.2, 0.5, 0.3)),
                levels=c("I", "II", "III"), ordered=TRUE)
## 02.02 Simulated binary response; not an actual therapy outcome
p_response <- stats::plogis(-0.3 + 0.35*(subtype=="Luminal-like") -
                            0.16*(tumor_cm-2.5))
response <- stats::rbinom(n, 1, p_response)
## 02.03 Synthetic follow-up and censoring; not observed cancer survival
event_time <- stats::rexp(n, rate=ifelse(subtype=="Basal-like", .10, .07))
censor_time <- stats::runif(n, min=2, max=15)
followup_months <- pmin(event_time, censor_time)
event <- as.integer(event_time <= censor_time)
## 02.04 Teaching count outcome with known positive person-time
exposure_years <- stats::runif(n, 0.5, 2)
toxicity_events <- stats::rpois(n, lambda=exposure_years *
                               ifelse(subtype=="Basal-like", 1.2, .8))
study <- data.frame(patient_id, subtype, age_years, tumor_cm,
                    erbb2_score, grade, response, followup_months,
                    event, exposure_years, toxicity_events)
## 02.05 Inject known missing outcomes for explicit reporting
study$erbb2_score[c(8L, 40L, 133L, 190L)] <- NA_real_
study$tumor_cm[c(9L, 141L)] <- NA_real_
data_origin <- "SIMULATED — no patients, no real assay or TCGA-BRCA data"
dictionary <- data.frame(
  variable=names(study),
  type=c("identifier","factor","numeric","numeric","numeric","ordinal",
         "binary","numeric","binary","numeric","integer count"),
  unit=c("ID","fictional label","years","cm","arbitrary score","grade",
         "0/1","months","0/1","years","event count"),
  stringsAsFactors=FALSE
)
present(dictionary, "Synthetic data dictionary")
```

# 03 Admission, units, missingness and cohort flow

```{r validation}
## 03.01 Fail closed on schema, ID, and range violations
stopifnot(nrow(study)==n, !anyNA(study$patient_id),
          !anyDuplicated(study$patient_id), identical(levels(study$subtype),names(pal)))
stopifnot(all(study$response %in% c(0L,1L)),
          all(study$event %in% c(0L,1L)),
          all(study$toxicity_events >= 0L),
          all(study$toxicity_events==floor(study$toxicity_events)),
          all(study$exposure_years > 0), all(study$followup_months > 0))
stopifnot(all(is.finite(as.matrix(study[c("age_years","tumor_cm","erbb2_score",
  "followup_months","exposure_years","toxicity_events")])) |
  is.na(as.matrix(study[c("age_years","tumor_cm","erbb2_score",
  "followup_months","exposure_years","toxicity_events")]))))
## 03.02 Missingness with explicit total-N denominator
missing_report <- data.frame(variable=names(study),
                             total_n=nrow(study),
                             observed_n=colSums(!is.na(study)),
                             missing_n=colSums(is.na(study)))
missing_report$missing_pct <- 100*missing_report$missing_n/missing_report$total_n
present(missing_report, "Missingness by variable")
## 03.03 Document complete cases only at the analysis that requires them
```

# 04 Descriptive and distributional statistics

```{r descriptive-summary}
## 04.01 Numeric summaries: n, missing, mean/SD, median/Q1/Q3/IQR
## This workbook uses type-7 quartiles explicitly. Biomedical methods 8e section 2.4
## illustrates type 2; for Biomedical methods replication opt into the separate
## biostat_descriptive_contract.R helper. Never silently switch conventions.
summ_num <- function(x, label) {
  total <- length(x); y <- x[!is.na(x)]; z <- length(y)
  q <- if(z) as.numeric(stats::quantile(y,c(.25,.75),type=7)) else c(NA_real_,NA_real_)
  data.frame(variable=label,total_n=total,observed_n=z,missing_n=total-z,
             mean=if(z)mean(y)else NA_real_,
             sd=if(z>1)stats::sd(y)else NA_real_,
             median=if(z)stats::median(y)else NA_real_,
             q1=q[1],q3=q[2],iqr=q[2]-q[1],
             min=if(z)min(y)else NA_real_,
             max=if(z)max(y)else NA_real_)
}
numeric_summary <- do.call(rbind,lapply(c("age_years","tumor_cm","erbb2_score"),
                                       function(v) summ_num(study[[v]],v)))
present(numeric_summary,"Descriptive statistics; sample SD and type-7 quartiles")
## 04.02 Categorical totals: do not confuse total and valid-case percentages
category_table <- as.data.frame(table(study$subtype, useNA="ifany"))
names(category_table) <- c("subtype","n")
category_table$pct_total <- 100*category_table$n/nrow(study)
present(category_table,"Synthetic subtype counts; denominator is all rows")
```

```{r distribution-graphics, fig.width=9, fig.height=5, fig.keep='all'}
## 04.03 Distribution (histogram) and individual observations (box-jitter)
plot_data <- study[!is.na(study$erbb2_score), , drop=FALSE]
p_hist <- ggplot2::ggplot(plot_data,ggplot2::aes(x=erbb2_score,fill=subtype))+
  ggplot2::geom_histogram(bins=22,alpha=.65,position="identity",color="white")+
  ggplot2::scale_fill_manual(values=pal)+ggplot2::theme_classic()+
  ggplot2::labs(title="Synthetic ERBB2 distribution",
    subtitle=sprintf("Observed n=%d; missing=%d",nrow(plot_data),
                     sum(is.na(study$erbb2_score))),
    x="ERBB2 expression (arbitrary score)",y="Specimen count",fill="Fictional subtype")
print(p_hist)
p_box <- ggplot2::ggplot(plot_data,ggplot2::aes(subtype,erbb2_score,fill=subtype))+
  ggplot2::geom_boxplot(width=.48,outlier.shape=NA)+
  ggplot2::geom_point(ggplot2::aes(color=subtype),
    position=ggplot2::position_jitter(width=.12,height=0,seed=params$seed),alpha=.35)+
  ggplot2::scale_fill_manual(values=pal)+ggplot2::scale_color_manual(values=pal)+
  ggplot2::theme_classic()+ggplot2::theme(legend.position="none")+
  ggplot2::labs(title="Synthetic ERBB2 by subtype",
    subtitle=sprintf("n=%d complete expression measurements",nrow(plot_data)),
    x="Fictional subtype",y="ERBB2 expression (arbitrary score)",
    caption="Whiskers are 1.5 × IQR conventions, not confidence intervals.")
print(p_box)
```

# 05 Test-selection logic — read before applying any method

| Outcome and design | Example / estimand | Candidate analysis | Critical gate |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Single continuous sample | Mean score versus predeclared reference | One-sample t or justified robust alternative | Independent units, reference value, distribution |
| Two independent continuous groups | Mean ERBB2 difference | Welch t; Wilcoxon rank-sum for rank/distribution question | Independence; Wilcoxon not automatically median test |
| Paired continuous samples | Within-patient marker change | Paired t; paired Wilcoxon | Correct matching, distribution of *differences* |
| Three or more independent groups | Continuous score across grades | Welch one-way ANOVA; Kruskal–Wallis | Omnibus test then prespecified comparisons |
| Categorical vs categorical | Response by subtype | Chi-square/Fisher exact | Expected counts, sampling model, effect size |
| Continuous associations | Tumor size with marker score | Pearson/Spearman | Linearity/outliers or monotonicity, no causation |
| Adjusted continuous outcome | Marker with size, age, subtype | Linear regression | Residuals, functional form, independence |
| Binary outcome | Response probability | Logistic regression | Events, separation, confounding and OR interpretation |
| Event count with exposure | Toxicity incidence | Poisson rate model / NB sensitivity | Offset, equidispersion, excess zeros |
| Time to event | Synthetic event hazard | Kaplan–Meier / log-rank / Cox | Censoring, time origin, PH assumption |
| Repeated measurements | Within-person score trend | Paired methods / mixed model | Correlated rows; patient-level ID |
| Classifier discrimination | Fictional response classification | ROC / AUC, calibration | No leakage, held-out samples, prevalence |
| Multiple genes/features | Many exploratory associations | Multiple-testing adjustment | Family definition and false discovery rate |
| Resampling | Mean difference uncertainty | Subject-level bootstrap | Resample independent units; no CI fabrication |
| Complex survey | Weighted population estimand | survey-aware methods | Valid weights, PSUs, strata; not demonstrated here |

**Researcher's workflow:** identify observation grain → sampling and assignment → outcome scale → estimand → model/test → diagnostics → effect/CI → interpretation. Tests below are *alternative demonstrations*, not a directive to apply every test to the same hypothesis.

# 06 Independent continuous comparisons

```{r continuous-tests}
## 06.01 Two independent subtype groups; Welch does not assume equal variance
a <- plot_data$erbb2_score[plot_data$subtype=="Luminal-like"]
b <- plot_data$erbb2_score[plot_data$subtype=="Basal-like"]
stopifnot(length(a)>=2L,length(b)>=2L)
welch <- stats::t.test(b,a,var.equal=FALSE,conf.level=.95)
welch_tab <- data.frame(contrast="Basal minus Luminal",difference=mean(b)-mean(a),
                       t=unname(welch$statistic),df=unname(welch$parameter),
                       lower=welch$conf.int[1],upper=welch$conf.int[2],
                       p=welch$p.value)
present(welch_tab,"Welch mean comparison; negative difference means basal score lower")
## 06.02 Rank-sum asks a rank/distribution question, not always median equality
rank_test <- stats::wilcox.test(b,a,exact=FALSE)
present(data.frame(method="Wilcoxon rank-sum",
                   statistic=unname(rank_test$statistic),p=rank_test$p.value),
        "Supplemental rank/distribution comparison")
## 06.03 One-sample test requires a justified *predeclared* benchmark
teaching_reference <- 12
one_sample <- stats::t.test(a,mu=teaching_reference)
present(data.frame(reference=teaching_reference,observed_mean=mean(a),
                   lower=one_sample$conf.int[1],upper=one_sample$conf.int[2],
                   p=one_sample$p.value),
        "Illustrative one-sample benchmark, not a clinical cutoff")
```

The Welch example estimates a mean difference; the rank-sum example compares rank distributions. The one-sample reference is invented solely to illustrate syntax and cannot be treated as a diagnostic threshold.

# 07 Three-group continuous comparison and post hoc multiplicity

```{r three-group-tests}
## 07.01 Grade creates three example groups; exploratory only
grades <- as.factor(study$grade)
grade_data <- data.frame(score=study$erbb2_score,grade=grades)
grade_data <- grade_data[stats::complete.cases(grade_data),,drop=FALSE]
anova_welch <- stats::oneway.test(score~grade,data=grade_data,var.equal=FALSE)
kw <- stats::kruskal.test(score~grade,data=grade_data)
present(data.frame(test=c("Welch one-way ANOVA","Kruskal-Wallis"),
 statistic=c(unname(anova_welch$statistic),unname(kw$statistic)),
 p=c(anova_welch$p.value,kw$p.value)),"Omnibus grade comparisons")
## 07.02 Post hoc comparisons are conditional on a declared question
pairwise_grade <- stats::pairwise.t.test(grade_data$score,grade_data$grade,
                                        p.adjust.method="holm",pool.sd=FALSE)
print(pairwise_grade)
```

Welch ANOVA targets differences among means under unequal variances. Kruskal–Wallis compares rank distributions; neither identifies which pairs differ without follow-up. The paired comparisons shown use Holm multiplicity control; unequal-variance pairwise Welch tests are not the same as the omnibus statistic.

# 08 Categorical comparisons: Chi-square, Fisher and two proportions

```{r categorical-tests}
## 08.01 Binary response by fictional subtype; check expected cells
response_table <- table(study$subtype,
                        factor(study$response,levels=c(0,1),labels=c("No","Yes")))
print(response_table)
chi <- suppressWarnings(stats::chisq.test(response_table,correct=FALSE))
use_fisher <- any(chi$expected < 5)
association <- if (use_fisher) stats::fisher.test(response_table) else chi
present(data.frame(method=if(use_fisher)"Fisher exact" else "Pearson Chi-square",
                   statistic=if(use_fisher)NA_real_ else unname(chi$statistic),
                   p=association$p.value),"Response × subtype association")
## 08.02 Report risk per group and crude risk difference, not p alone
risk <- response_table[,"Yes"]/rowSums(response_table)
present(data.frame(subtype=names(risk),events=as.integer(response_table[,"Yes"]),
                   total=as.integer(rowSums(response_table)),
                   risk=as.numeric(risk)),"Observed synthetic response proportions")
```

A chi-square test evaluates association; Fisher is used when sparse expected counts make the asymptotic approximation questionable. Risk is a sample proportion and not a hazard. Logistic regression below estimates *odds*, not risk.

# 09 Continuous association and adjusted linear regression

```{r correlation-and-linear}
## 09.01 Pairwise complete observations for this exact estimand
xy <- study[stats::complete.cases(study[c("tumor_cm","erbb2_score")]),,drop=FALSE]
pearson <- stats::cor.test(xy$tumor_cm,xy$erbb2_score,method="pearson")
spearman <- stats::cor.test(xy$tumor_cm,xy$erbb2_score,
                            method="spearman",exact=FALSE)
present(data.frame(method=c("Pearson","Spearman"),
 estimate=c(unname(pearson$estimate),unname(spearman$estimate)),
 p=c(pearson$p.value,spearman$p.value),n=nrow(xy)),
 "Association of synthetic tumor size and ERBB2 score")
## 09.02 Prespecified covariates; estimates are adjusted associations
linear_fit <- stats::lm(erbb2_score~subtype+tumor_cm+age_years,data=study,
                       na.action=stats::na.omit)
linear_coef <- as.data.frame(summary(linear_fit)$coefficients)
linear_coef$term <- rownames(linear_coef);rownames(linear_coef)<-NULL
present(linear_coef[,c("term","Estimate","Std. Error","t value","Pr(>|t|)")],
        "Adjusted linear regression coefficient table")
```

```{r linear-diagnostics, fig.width=8, fig.height=5}
## 09.03 Residual-versus-fitted and Q-Q diagnostics, not a blanket pass
op <- graphics::par(mfrow=c(1,2))
graphics::plot(stats::fitted(linear_fit),stats::residuals(linear_fit),
               xlab="Fitted ERBB2 score",ylab="Residual",main="Residuals vs fitted")
graphics::abline(h=0,lty=2,col="#D55E00")
stats::qqnorm(stats::residuals(linear_fit),main="Normal Q-Q residuals")
stats::qqline(stats::residuals(linear_fit),col="#0072B2")
graphics::par(op)
```

Linear coefficients are conditional differences in mean synthetic score; inspect nonlinear patterns, leverage, heteroskedasticity, clustering, collinearity and study justification before interpreting real-world fits. Correlation does not imply causation.

# 10 Binary-outcome logistic regression

```{r logistic-regression}
## 10.01 Probability model; explicit binary coding 0/1
logit_fit <- stats::glm(response~subtype+tumor_cm+age_years,
                        data=study,family=stats::binomial(),
                        na.action=stats::na.omit)
logit_mat <- summary(logit_fit)$coefficients
logit_ci <- stats::confint.default(logit_fit)
logit_or <- data.frame(term=rownames(logit_mat),
                      odds_ratio=exp(stats::coef(logit_fit)),
                      lower=exp(logit_ci[,1]),upper=exp(logit_ci[,2]),
                      p=logit_mat[,4],row.names=NULL)
present(logit_or,"Adjusted logistic odds ratios, Wald 95% confidence intervals")
## 10.02 Diagnostics: events and fitted-probability boundaries
stopifnot(all(stats::fitted(logit_fit)>0),all(stats::fitted(logit_fit)<1))
present(data.frame(model_n=stats::nobs(logit_fit),
                   events=sum(stats::model.response(stats::model.frame(logit_fit))==1),
                   min_pred=min(stats::fitted(logit_fit)),
                   max_pred=max(stats::fitted(logit_fit))),
        "Model sample and prediction range")
```

An odds ratio is not a risk ratio. In real studies assess separation, sparse events, positivity, predictive calibration, confounding and how continuous predictors enter the log odds. Wald intervals here are demonstration defaults, not universally optimal.

# 11 Count outcomes, offsets and dispersion

```{r poisson-model}
## 11.01 Rates require an exposure offset; positive exposure validated above
pois_fit <- stats::glm(toxicity_events~subtype+age_years+
                         offset(log(exposure_years)),
                       family=stats::poisson(),data=study)
dispersion <- sum(stats::residuals(pois_fit,type="pearson")^2) /
              stats::df.residual(pois_fit)
pois_beta <- summary(pois_fit)$coefficients
pois_ci <- stats::confint.default(pois_fit)
present(data.frame(term=rownames(pois_beta),
                   rate_ratio=exp(stats::coef(pois_fit)),
                   lower=exp(pois_ci[,1]),upper=exp(pois_ci[,2]),
                   p=pois_beta[,4],row.names=NULL),
        "Poisson incidence rate ratios and Wald intervals")
present(data.frame(pearson_dispersion=dispersion,
                   observed_zero_fraction=mean(study$toxicity_events==0)),
        "Poisson dispersion and observed zeros")
```

Poisson uses an event *count*, with log(person-time) offset and equidispersion assumption. Check time at risk and event definitions. Overdispersion can require quasi-Poisson, negative binomial or another prespecified framework; a quasi-Poisson scale adjustment does not estimate a separate NB dispersion parameter. Do not confuse counts with rates or use a Poisson count model on continuous measurements.

# 12 Survival analysis: Kaplan–Meier, log-rank and Cox

```{r survival-analysis, fig.width=8, fig.height=5}
## 12.01 survival is optional; document a skipped analysis if unavailable
if (requireNamespace("survival",quietly=TRUE)) {
  S <- survival::Surv(time=study$followup_months,event=study$event)
  km <- survival::survfit(S~subtype,data=study)
  graphics::plot(km,col=unname(pal),lwd=2,mark.time=TRUE,
                 xlab="Synthetic follow-up (months)",ylab="Event-free proportion",
                 main="Synthetic Kaplan-Meier curves")
  graphics::legend("bottomleft",legend=names(pal),col=unname(pal),lwd=2,bty="n")
  lr <- survival::survdiff(S~subtype,data=study)
  logrank_p <- stats::pchisq(lr$chisq,df=length(lr$n)-1,lower.tail=FALSE)
  cox_fit <- survival::coxph(S~subtype+age_years,data=study,x=TRUE)
  cox_ci <- stats::confint(cox_fit)
  present(data.frame(term=names(stats::coef(cox_fit)),
                     hazard_ratio=exp(stats::coef(cox_fit)),
                     lower=exp(cox_ci[,1]),upper=exp(cox_ci[,2]),
                     row.names=NULL),"Cox adjusted hazard ratios")
  present(data.frame(logrank_chisq=lr$chisq,p=logrank_p),
          "Log-rank test: unadjusted curve comparison")
  print(survival::cox.zph(cox_fit))
} else {
  cat("Survival module not executed: install 'survival' before this optional module.\n")
}
```

Define event, competing events, time zero, administrative censoring and proportional-hazards diagnostics. Kaplan–Meier handles right censoring, not informative loss to follow-up by fiat; a hazard ratio is not a risk ratio or difference in survival probability. A Cox PH test is diagnostic, not definitive validation.

# 13 Paired and repeated-measure analyses

```{r paired-and-repeated}
## 13.01 Two synthetic measurements from the SAME patient
## Use a shared patient baseline so the two visits are correlated.
baseline_score <- stats::rnorm(n,mean=40,sd=6)
followup_score <- baseline_score + stats::rnorm(n,mean=2,sd=3)
repeated <- data.frame(
 patient_id=rep(study$patient_id,each=2L),
 visit=factor(rep(c("Baseline","Follow-up"),times=n),
              levels=c("Baseline","Follow-up")),
 score=as.vector(t(cbind(baseline_score,followup_score)))
)
wide <- reshape(repeated,idvar="patient_id",timevar="visit",direction="wide")
stopifnot(nrow(wide)==n,!anyDuplicated(wide$patient_id),
          all(c("score.Baseline", "score.Follow-up") %in% names(wide)))
difference <- wide[["score.Follow-up"]]-wide[["score.Baseline"]]
paired_t <- stats::t.test(wide[["score.Follow-up"]],wide[["score.Baseline"]],paired=TRUE)
paired_rank <- stats::wilcox.test(wide[["score.Follow-up"]],wide[["score.Baseline"]],
                                  paired=TRUE,exact=FALSE)
present(data.frame(n_pairs=length(difference),mean_change=mean(difference),
                   lower=paired_t$conf.int[1],upper=paired_t$conf.int[2],
                   paired_t_p=paired_t$p.value,paired_wilcoxon_p=paired_rank$p.value),
        "Paired mean change and signed-rank sensitivity analysis")
## 13.02 Optional patient random intercept for two repeated observations
if (requireNamespace("nlme",quietly=TRUE)) {
  mixed <- nlme::lme(score~visit,random=~1|patient_id,data=repeated)
  present(data.frame(term=rownames(summary(mixed)$tTable),
                     summary(mixed)$tTable,row.names=NULL),
          "Optional repeated-measure random-intercept model")
} else cat("Mixed-model module not executed: 'nlme' is unavailable.\n")
```

Paired analyses test within-patient change, not two independent groups. Two visits do not establish the right covariance structure for longer longitudinal trajectories. For repeated visits, account for within-person correlation, informative dropout and irregular follow-up; use appropriate mixed models or marginal models with justified design.

# 14 Classification metrics and leakage-aware evaluation

```{r classifier-evaluation}
## 14.01 Method demonstration only: use a frozen held-out set
## Synthetic response prediction has no clinical predictive validity.
set.seed(params$seed+1L)
idx <- sample(seq_len(nrow(study)),size=floor(.7*nrow(study)))
## Freeze the assignment before outcome-complete-case filtering; never
## reassign a participant after inspecting prediction labels or results.
train_ids <- study$patient_id[idx]
test_ids <- study$patient_id[-idx]
stopifnot(!anyDuplicated(train_ids), !anyDuplicated(test_ids),
          !any(train_ids %in% test_ids),
          length(train_ids)+length(test_ids)==nrow(study))
train <- study[idx,,drop=FALSE];test_set <- study[-idx,,drop=FALSE]
train <- train[stats::complete.cases(train[c("response","subtype","age_years",
                                            "tumor_cm")]),,drop=FALSE]
test_set <- test_set[stats::complete.cases(test_set[c("response","subtype",
                                                    "age_years","tumor_cm")]),,drop=FALSE]
stopifnot(nrow(train)>0L, nrow(test_set)>0L,
          !any(train$patient_id %in% test_set$patient_id),
          all(train$patient_id %in% train_ids),
          all(test_set$patient_id %in% test_ids),
          all(c(0L,1L) %in% train$response),
          all(c(0L,1L) %in% test_set$response))
classifier <- stats::glm(response~subtype+age_years+tumor_cm,
                         data=train,family=stats::binomial())
probs <- stats::predict(classifier,newdata=test_set,type="response")
pred <- as.integer(probs>=.5)
tp <- sum(pred==1 & test_set$response==1)
tn <- sum(pred==0 & test_set$response==0)
fp <- sum(pred==1 & test_set$response==0)
fn <- sum(pred==0 & test_set$response==1)
metric <- function(num,den)if(den>0)num/den else NA_real_
pred_metrics <- data.frame(test_n=nrow(test_set),TP=tp,TN=tn,FP=fp,FN=fn,
 sensitivity=metric(tp,tp+fn),specificity=metric(tn,tn+fp),
 ppv=metric(tp,tp+fp),npv=metric(tn,tn+fn),
 brier=mean((probs-test_set$response)^2))
present(pred_metrics,"Synthetic held-out classification metrics")
## 14.02 Base-R AUC is an empirical ranking statistic, 0.5=random chance
auc_rank <- function(p,y) {
 pos <- which(y==1);neg <- which(y==0)
 if(!length(pos)||!length(neg))return(NA_real_)
 ranks <- rank(p,ties.method="average")
 (sum(ranks[pos])-length(pos)*(length(pos)+1)/2)/(length(pos)*length(neg))
}
cat("Held-out empirical AUC:",fmt(auc_rank(probs,test_set$response)),"\n")
```

AUC estimates rank discrimination; Brier score evaluates probability prediction error. Neither proves calibration, external validity, or clinical utility. In genuine studies, split by patient/site/time as appropriate, prevent leakage and tune models **inside** the training data only; use untouched test data once. For very small or sparse subsets, report undefined denominators explicitly.

# 15 Bootstrap effect uncertainty and multiple-testing control

```{r bootstrap-and-multiplicity}
## 15.01 Resample subjects within independent synthetic subtype groups
set.seed(params$seed+2L)
B <- 1000L
boot_diff <- replicate(B,mean(sample(b,length(b),replace=TRUE))-
                         mean(sample(a,length(a),replace=TRUE)))
boot_ci <- stats::quantile(boot_diff,c(.025,.975),names=FALSE,type=7)
present(data.frame(replicates=B,estimate=mean(b)-mean(a),
                   lower=boot_ci[1],upper=boot_ci[2]),
        "Stratified subject bootstrap percentile CI (illustrative)")
## 15.02 Artificial four-feature exploratory family for BH FDR
feature_data <- data.frame(
 ERBB2=study$erbb2_score,
 marker_B=stats::rnorm(n,0,1),
 marker_C=stats::rnorm(n,.5,1),
 marker_D=stats::rnorm(n,-.5,1)
)
features <- names(feature_data)
p_raw <- vapply(features,function(v) {
 x <- feature_data[[v]]
 z <- !is.na(x)
 stats::t.test(x[z & study$subtype=="Basal-like"],
               x[z & study$subtype=="Luminal-like"])$p.value
},numeric(1))
present(data.frame(feature=features,raw_p=as.numeric(p_raw),
                   BH_FDR=stats::p.adjust(p_raw,method="BH"),
                   Holm=stats::p.adjust(p_raw,method="holm")),
        "Multiplicity: explicit family of four simulated features")
```

Percentile bootstrap requires independently resampled units and may be inadequate for skewed or boundary estimands; use a protocol-appropriate interval where needed. BH controls the expected false discovery *proportion under its assumptions*, not the probability a particular claim is false. A four-feature educational example is not a genome-wide expression pipeline.

# 16 Methodology, reporting and computational audit

```{r methods-audit}
## 16.01 Machine-readable counts that feed the interpretation
audit <- data.frame(
  source_class=data_origin, seed=params$seed,
  baseline_N=nrow(study), independent_subjects=length(unique(study$patient_id)),
  erbb2_observed=sum(!is.na(study$erbb2_score)),
  erbb2_missing=sum(is.na(study$erbb2_score)),
  linear_model_n=stats::nobs(linear_fit),
  logistic_model_n=stats::nobs(logit_fit),
  poisson_model_n=stats::nobs(pois_fit),
  repeated_records=nrow(repeated),
  heldout_n=nrow(test_set)
)
present(audit,"Computational provenance and analysis-specific denominators")
cat("\nSession provenance:\n")
print(utils::sessionInfo())
```

# 17 Computed example results narrative

Among `r nrow(study)` synthetic breast cancer observations, `r sum(!is.na(study$erbb2_score))`
had an observed fictional ERBB2 score; `r sum(is.na(study$erbb2_score))` were missing.
The independent-group Welch estimate (basal-like minus luminal-like) was
`r fmt(mean(b)-mean(a),2)` arbitrary score units (95% CI
`r fmt(welch$conf.int[1],2)` to `r fmt(welch$conf.int[2],2)`),
t(`r fmt(unname(welch$parameter),2)`)=`r fmt(unname(welch$statistic),2)`,
p=`r format.pval(welch$p.value,digits=3)`.
The simulated within-person score change averaged `r fmt(mean(difference),2)`
arbitrary score units across `r length(difference)` complete synthetic pairs.

These numerical results are generated at render time; they are **not breast cancer findings**.
No statistical significance result alone establishes practical or clinical importance.

# 18 Review gates and customization

1. Replace the fictional cohort with a single approved import and a verified dictionary.
2. Identify population, unit of analysis, inclusion/exclusion, independent patient identifiers, censoring, endpoint, exposures and clinical units.
3. Predeclare primary/secondary estimands, hypotheses, tests and multiplicity family. Use each section only where its question/design applies.
4. Record eligible, analyzed and missing counts per method. Never silently delete, impute or recode.
5. Assess distribution, independence, pairing, expected cells, regression functional form, dispersion, censoring, proportional hazards, prediction leakage and calibration as applicable.
6. Report each method's rationale, assumptions, estimator, test statistic, uncertainty, exact denominator, scientific meaning and limitations.
7. Source current repository helpers when available; keep Okabe–Ito mappings, documented seeds and readable plots.
8. Validate actual execution, inspect the knitted output and record the exact successful/failed commands. Knitting success is not scientific validation.

**Excluded advanced workflows requiring their own protocol:** genome-wide differential expression with raw RNA-seq counts (edgeR/DESeq2), batch correction, high-dimensional feature selection and nested CV, competing risks, causal inference, imputation, survey-weighted population inference, time-dependent Cox models, noninferiority, power/sample-size planning and external validation. These cannot be responsibly reduced to plug-in test snippets without study-specific assumptions.
